activities.title: Short vowel sort
materials: index cards or scraps of paper
parentPrompts: Write one vowel (a, e, i, o, u) at the top of each of 5 sheets. Say each short sound with your child: apple, egg, itch, octopus, up.
Write 15 simple words on cards, 3 for each vowel (for example: map, bed, pig, hot, sun, hat, net, lid, dog, mud, cap, pen, zip, box, bus). Mix them up.
Your child reads each card aloud, says the vowel sound, and places it on the matching sheet. Ask: "How do you know which sound the vowel makes?"
Finish by having your child say a new word for each vowel and write one of them. Check: they can read most cards without long pauses and match the vowel sound correctly.

subject: literacy
title: Silent e makes a say its name

activities.title: Silent e makes a say its name
materials: a small card with the letter e
parentPrompts: Write the word "cap" and have your child read it. Then place the e card at the end to make "cape." Ask: "What happened to the vowel sound?" (The a now says its name, and the e stays silent.)
Try more pairs the same way: tap/tape, mad/made, hat/hate, can/cane, plan/plane. Your child reads each pair aloud.
Write 6 a_e words on a page (cake, gate, name, lake, game, wave) and have your child draw a small line under each a_e pattern, then read the list twice.
Have your child write 3 sentences, each using one a_e word. Read them together. Check: they can tell you the e is silent and changes the sound of the a.

subject: literacy
title: Silent e with i, o, and u

activities.title: Silent e with i, o, and u
materials: a card with the letter e
parentPrompts: Review: say "cap, cape." Tell your child silent e works with the other vowels too.
Use the e card on these pairs and read each aloud: kit/kite, hop/hope, cub/cube, bit/bite, not/note, cut/cute, rod/rode.
Make three columns (i_e, o_e, u_e). Say a word, your child writes it in the right column: bike, nose, tube, five, bone, mule, slide, stone.
Play "say it, spell it, change it": you say "hop," they spell it, then add an e and say the new word. Check: they correctly say the long vowel sound for at least 6 of 8 words.

activities.title: Read it again, smoother
parentPrompts: Read this short passage aloud once slowly while your child follows: "Ben has a red kite. The wind is strong today. Ben runs up the hill and lets go of the string. The kite goes up, up, up! It dips and spins like a bird. Ben smiles." Write it out on paper first if you want your child to read from the page.
Your child reads it aloud. Mark any word that was tricky with a small dot. Help with those words, then have them read it again.
Read it a third time, this time asking your child to sound like they are telling a friend a story: pause at periods, and let their voice show the excitement at "up, up, up!"
On the chart, draw a smile for each read that felt smoother. Ask: "What changed from the first read to the third?" Check: reading gets smoother and more expressive with each reread.

activities.title: Write what happened
parentPrompts: Ask your child to tell you about something they did recently, such as a trip, a game, or a meal. Listen for first, next, and last.
Draw three boxes on the page and label them First, Next, and Last. Have your child sketch each part of their event.

Under each picture, your child writes one or two sentences using the words first, next, and last. Remind them to start with a capital letter and end with a period. Add one detail that tells how they felt.
Read it aloud together. Ask: "Does it have a beginning, a middle, and an ending?" Check: they use time-order words and at least one feeling word.

activities.title: Doubles facts
materials: 10 small counters (buttons, coins, or dried beans)
parentPrompts: Show 3 counters in a row and 3 more under them. Ask: "What is 3 + 3?" Explain that doubles are two of the same number.
Have your child make and say doubles from 1 + 1 to 10 + 10 using counters, then write each fact on paper (for example, 7 + 7 = 14). Keep counters away from young siblings and mouths.
Play "double it": say a number from 1 to 10 and your child says the double fast. Do 10 rounds.
Ask: "Which doubles are easy for you? Which are hard?" Check: they can answer most doubles up to 10 + 10 without counting by ones.

activities.title: Make ten to add
materials: a ten-frame drawn on paper (2 rows of 5 boxes)
parentPrompts: Put 8 counters on the ten-frame. Ask: "How many more to make ten?" (2)
Show 8 + 5. Move 2 counters from the 5 to fill the frame, leaving 3 more. Say: "8 + 2 is 10, and 10 + 3 is 13."
Try 9 + 4, 7 + 6, and 8 + 7 the same way. Your child moves counters and says the steps out loud.
Ask them to try one without counters. Check: they can break apart one number to make ten, then add the rest.

activities.title: Near doubles
parentPrompts: Review a double, such as 6 + 6 = 12. Then ask: "If 6 + 6 is 12, what is 6 + 7?" (One more, so 13.)
Practice near doubles: 5 + 6, 7 + 8, 8 + 9, 4 + 5. Use counters to show the double and then add one more.
Roll a die twice (or choose two numbers) and decide if the facts are a double, a near double, or neither. Solve them.
Check: they use a known double to solve a near-double fact.

activities.title: Odd and even numbers
parentPrompts: Show 6 objects. Have your child make pairs. If none are left over, the number is even. Do the same with 7: one is left over, so 7 is odd.
Test numbers from 1 to 20. Your child pairs the objects and records each number in an Odd or Even column.
Look for a pattern: ask, "What digits do even numbers end in?" (0, 2, 4, 6, 8)
Challenge: "Is 17 odd or even? How do you know?" Check: they can use pairing or the last digit to decide.

activities.title: Story problems
parentPrompts: Read aloud: "Sam has 9 stickers. He gets 6 more. How many does he have now?" Have your child act it out with counters and write a number sentence: 9 + 6 = 15.
Read a take-away story: "There are 14 birds on a fence. 5 fly away. How many are left?" Draw it and write 14 - 5 = 9.
Take turns making up your own story problems with real things at home. Your child solves yours and you solve theirs.
Ask: "How did you know whether to add or subtract?" Check: they match the story to the right operation and write an equation.

activities.title: Property hunt and sort
materials: 10 to 15 household items (a spoon, a sponge, a rock, a cup, a sock, a coin, a leaf)
parentPrompts: Place the items on a table. Ask: "How would you describe each one?" Collect words like hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, shiny.
Choose a property, such as hard or soft. Your child sorts the items into two groups. Ask: "What did you notice?"
Sort again by a different property, such as shiny or dull, or bendy or stiff. Note that the same item can go in different groups.
Ask: "Which property helps us decide what an object is good for?" Check: they use properties to describe and sort materials.

activities.title: Float or sink
materials: a large bowl or tub of water
small objects (cork, coin, plastic spoon, sponge, rock, wooden block)
parentPrompts: Set up the water on a towel. Ask your child to predict whether each object will float or sink and record the predictions.
Test one object at a time, then note the result. Stay with the water and never leave a child alone near it.
Compare predictions to results. Ask: "What do the floaters have in common?" Remember that size alone does not decide it. A big ship floats and a small pebble sinks.
Check: they can say that materials have properties that affect whether they float.

activities.title: Which material soaks up water?
parentPrompts: Put each material on a tray. Ask which will soak up water best, and record the guesses.
Place the same amount of water (one spoon) on each material and watch what happens.
Record which materials absorbed water and which let it sit on top. Look at the data table together.
Ask: "Which material would you use to clean a spill? Why?" Check: they pick a material based on test results.

activities.title: A map of my room
parentPrompts: Stand at the doorway of a room. Ask your child to look down from above in their mind, as a bird would. Explain that a map is a drawing of a place from above.
Place a few objects on the floor. Draw the room as a big rectangle on paper, then draw simple shapes for the bed, door, and window.
Add a title, then draw a small box with a key that shows what each shape means.
Ask: "Where is the door on your map?" Check: they can place objects on a map in the right spot and explain the key.

activities.title: Symbols and keys
parentPrompts: Show a map from a book or print one. Point to the symbols and the key. Explain that a symbol is a small picture that stands for a real thing.
Have your child make a map of a make-believe island with 5 symbols (a tree, a house, a lake, a road, a bridge) and a key to explain them.
Swap maps with a family member who has to find three things using only the key.
Check: they can use a map key to find a place and make symbols that make sense.
